PASSO 1: o objeto direto é a coisa ou a: STEP 1: the direct object is the thing or person that receives the verb's action. To find it, ask «what?» or «who?» right after the verb: in «Compré el libro», I bought what? El libro. STEP 2: to avoid repeating it, swap the object for a pronoun that agrees with it in gender and number: «lo» (masculine, singular), «la» (feminine, singular), «los» (masculine, plural), and «las» (feminine, plural). «¿Compraste el libro? — Sí, lo compré.» STEP 3: the pronoun comes before the conjugated verb, as its own separate word with no hyphen: «Lo compré», «La veo», «Las busco». STEP 4: in the negative, «no» comes before the pronoun: «No lo tengo», «No la encuentro». STEP 5: with an infinitive, there are two equally correct positions: before the conjugated verb («Lo quiero comprar») or attached to the end of the infinitive («Quiero comprarlo»), with no hyphen. STEP 6: with the pretérito perfecto, the pronoun comes before «haber»: «Lo he visto», «No la he encontrado». STEP 7: when the object is a person, the personal «a» disappears along with the name: «Veo a Ana» becomes «La veo». STEP 8: Spanish never lets you drop this pronoun once the object has already been mentioned: «¿Viste la película? — Sí, la vi».
o português escrito tem «o, a, os, as» (: English object pronouns (it, him, her, them) are required too, just like Spanish, so the underlying habit of never dropping the object isn't new ground — English speakers already do this instinctively. What genuinely is new is word order: English object pronouns always sit after the verb («I bought it», «I saw her»), while Spanish puts the pronoun before the conjugated verb («Lo compré», «La vi») or attaches it directly onto an infinitive with no space and no hyphen («comprarlo») — a position English has no equivalent for at all.

Me, te, nos, os, usted e o «lo» neutro: Me, te, nos, os, usted, and the neuter «lo»
PASSO 1: quando o objeto direto é a pess: STEP 1: when the direct object is the speaker or the listener, the pronouns are «me» (me), «te» (you, tú), «nos» (us), and «os» (you-all, vosotros). «Me llamas», «Te espero», «Nos invitan», «Os visito». STEP 2: «usted» and «ustedes» follow the third-person pattern: «Lo llamo mañana, señor Ruiz» and «La ayudo, señora». For ustedes: «Los llamo» or «Las llamo». STEP 3: «me», «te», «nos», and «os» also work as indirect objects; only the third person changes. Lesson 24 covers the indirect object. STEP 4: «lo» can also stand in for an idea rather than a noun. This is called the «neuter lo»: «No lo sé» (I don't know), «Ya lo sabía» (I already knew that), «Lo entiendo» (I understand), «Lo siento» (I'm sorry). «Lo siento» is a fixed phrase for apologizing — it isn't literally «I feel it». STEP 5: with «ser» and «estar», it's common to echo the adjective with «lo»: «¿Estás cansado? — Sí, lo estoy» (are you tired? —Yes, I am). That sounds more natural than the bare «Sí, estoy». STEP 6: verbs that commonly take a direct object: llamar, esperar, ayudar, visitar, invitar, acompañar, conocer, escuchar, mirar, buscar. STEP 7: «esperar» means both to wait for and to hope: «Te espero a las ocho» means «I'll wait for you at eight». «Buscar» means to look for or to go pick someone up: «Te busco en la estación» (I'll pick you up at the station). STEP 8: in Spain, for male people it's common to hear «le» instead of «lo» («le veo mañana»); this is called «leísmo», and it's accepted in Spain. This course uses «lo» and «la», and you'll be understood everywhere.
em português, «te espero» e «me liga» tê: English «I'll wait for you» and «call me» follow the same basic word order Spanish does for these forms, so «te espero» and «me llamas» feel familiar in structure. What has no real English counterpart is the neuter «lo»: English «I don't know» and «I understand» stand complete on their own, with nothing playing the role of an object, while Spanish prefers to anchor the idea to something with «lo sé» and «lo entiendo» — leaving it out isn't wrong exactly, but «lo» makes the sentence feel more complete and natural to a Spanish ear.

PASSO 1: com «ir a + infinitivo», «quere: STEP 1: with «ir a + infinitive», «querer + infinitive», «poder + infinitive», there are two positions: «Voy a comprarlo» or «Lo voy a comprar»; «Puedo verla» or «La puedo ver». STEP 2: picking one position over the other is just a matter of style; both are correct. What you never do is put the pronoun in the middle: «Voy lo a comprar». STEP 3: with the pretérito perfecto, the pronoun never attaches to the participle: «Lo he visto», never «He visto-lo». STEP 4: for emphasis, the object gets repeated at the start of the sentence: «A Ana la vi ayer» (Ana, I saw her yesterday) and «Ese libro lo compré en Madrid» (that book, I bought it in Madrid). This is completely natural in both speech and writing. STEP 5: useful false friends for this lesson. «Cola» means a line of people (at a bank or a checkout): «Vi a Marta en la cola». It's also the word for glue and for an animal's tail. In several Latin American countries, like Mexico, «fila» is more common for a line of people; both are understood everywhere. «Oficina» means «office», not an auto repair shop (which is «taller»). «Pegar» means to hit or to glue, not «to catch» — for catching the bus, use «tomar».
o português dos livros aceita «pretendo: English keeps its object pronoun fixed after the verb no matter what else is going on in the sentence, so the idea that Spanish gives you two equally correct spots — before the whole verb phrase, or stuck onto the infinitive — is new territory, not a choice English makes you face. What never changes, in either language, is that the pronoun can't float in the middle of a verb phrase: English would never say «I'm going it to buy» any more than Spanish allows «Voy lo a comprar», so that instinct does transfer directly.
